Mohammad Reza Pahlavi. The last Shah of Iran. Pahlavi ascended to the throne in nineteen forty-one after his father's forced abdication, inheriting a weakened state and gradually consolidating power. He pursued the White Revolution in the nineteen-sixties and seventies, a top-down modernization campaign including land reform, women's suffrage, and industrial expansion. Pahlavi aligned Iran with the United States and Israel, accepting Western military and economic presence, which angered nationalist and religious constituencies. He built up one of the largest militaries in the region, spending vast oil revenues on military hardware and development projects. He maintained a secret police force called SAVAK that suppressed dissent through torture and surveillance, radicalizing opposition movements. He attempted to minimize Islam's role in public life, earning opposition from Ayatollah Khomeini and other clerics who saw his policies as a betrayal of Iran's Islamic tradition. As the Islamic Revolution swept the country in nineteen seventy-nine, he fled Iran in January. He died in exile in Egypt in July nineteen eighty, dethroned and reviled. His legacy exemplifies the tension between modernization and cultural backlash, a tension that defined twentieth-century Middle Eastern politics. Khomeini became his nemesis and the architect of his ouster, establishing the Islamic Republic that replaced his secular monarchy.
